author: zdimension
text:
When you call a method on something in Rust, the method gets passed that something (as a parameter called self). But the method gets to choose whether it's by move/copy or by reference. Here, toggle gets the bool passed by mutable reference.

In effect, if x is a bool, doing x.toggle() is rewritten by the compiler as bool::toggle(&mut x), which can of course modify x.

If you declare a boolean without specifying the binding as mutable, you'd get a compiler error from trying to call this method. Moreover, if anything else had a reference to it at the same time, it would also cause a compiler error to call this method.

This is definitely something that Rust does a bit different than most other languages, but it's not anything specific to this method, booleans, or particularly new to the language. author: stusmall
text:
The big clue that'll jump out to any rust dev is the type signature:

pub const fn toggle(&mut self)

The "&mut" says that toggle takes a mutable reference to the instance it is called off of.  This is also called a mutable borrow.  You might think that would get buried in the program because you don't always check the type signature of every method you call, but there are a few reasons that muts really jump out in rust.  The languages immutable by default nature is one and the other is that several IDE have features to specifically draw attention to mutable instances/references.  It's a fairly common pattern in rust to have helper methods on a type that take a mutable reference or ownership of self.

TL;DR:  Rust's ownership model is very unique.  Once it clicks its the cat's pajamas, but experience in other languages don't map well to this part of the language.

author: epage
text:
Faster compile and smaller build-dir can be at odds with each other.

That said, this release includes some incremental improvements as well as the unused-dependency lint to help reduce wasted work within the ecosystem.

Some changes that have been or are about to be merged for upcoming releases

- We will be reducing the debug info generated for the `dev` profile which reduces build-dir size and speeds up builds. We've split off a `debug` profile for when that is needed.

- Cargo will be deleting the directory rustc writes before each invocation, avoiding the leaking of debug files when split-debug is enabled (default on Mac)

- rlibs for workspace members will no longer be copied from build-dir to target-dir which takes up extra space on systems without hardlinking or where we skip it (like Mac)

- redundant information in rlibs and rmeta's is going to be de-duplicated

Examples of further out changes

- This release includes the foundational work to add a build-dir GC

- Cross-workspace de-duplicating of build-dirs

- Cross-workspace build-dir cache

- Early cut off

author: dabinat
text:
I think the main reason Rust gets a bad reputation for compile times is that the compiler makes it very easy to shoot yourself in the foot. When I first started using Rust my compile times for release builds were around 7-8 mins. Then I tweaked some settings and split things up into smaller crates and got it to be under a minute, which was fine for me.

cargo check would still take a long time though, until I realized that I had a build script that was triggering more often that it should, causing Rust to throw out a lot of its work and redo it. Once I fixed that, cargo check was near-instant.

So as a Rust developer you can have decent compile times but only if you (and your dependencies) optimize for it. Hopefully at some point we’ll be able to stop having to think about it, but we’re not there yet.

author: barchar
text:
try disabling at least some debug-info for your dependencies.

use cargo's --timings option to identify the slow crates, then use measureme to figure where rustc is spending time.

try fiddling with detached debug-info, dwp files can be smaller than their constituent dwo files.

ensure really small "template wrappers" are inlined.

lower the number of compilation-units you use.

For incremental builds I have found it can _sometimes_ be effective to split out larger dependencies into a dynlib. You create a dylib crate that re-exports said dependencies and your executable depends on that. Ofc things like generics from the offending libraries will still end up in your executables; Though I think there is a way to mitigate this a little.

This mostly helps with link-time, and saving space if you have a bunch of executables (using the argv[0] trick will help more, though).

author: JoshTriplett
text:
The primary challenge in having a stable ABI is that we have generics. So, even if we never changed the calling conventions, an ABI is not as simple as exporting a symbol with the right name. We implement generics by providing MIR (our main intermediate representation) that gets compiled by the linking program for each instantiation of a generic.

Swift handles this through the equivalent of Rust's `dyn`. We could have a stable ABI that's based entirely on `dyn`. Such an ABI would have some limitations, since there are traits `dyn` can't represent (anything that's generic over something other than the type that implements the trait, which is quite common), though we're working on some of those.

Essentially, you wouldn't be able to have a `Vec<T>` in your ABI without either pinning down T or using something like `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`. Which is possible, but kind of awful.

We're still planning to ship a stable ABI at some point, but that gives a flavor for some of the kinds of problems we'd need to solve in order for that stable ABI to be useful.

(C++ typically handles generics by having types defined in header files, and those get compiled with the program consuming the library, which is effectively the same situation Rust is in. You could export symbols from a shared library for specific instantiation of a template, but people rarely do that.)

Essentially, you wouldn't be able to have a `Vec<T>` in your ABI without either pinning down T or using something like `Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>`. Which is possible, but kind of awful.
We're still planning to ship a stable ABI at some point, but that gives a flavor for some of the kinds of problems we'd need to solve in order for that stable ABI to be useful.
(C++ typically handles generics by having types defined in header files, and those get compiled with the program consuming the library, which is effectively the same situation Rust is in. You could export symbols from a shared library for specific instantiation of a template, but people rarely do that.)

Most of the reasons previously not to use Rust came down to the i) non-trivial learning curve, especially the ownership model, and ii) the (allegedly) overbearingly strict compiler that forces you to think through potential errors and solve them.

author: simonask
text:
You stumbled upon my pet peeve.

Both C and C++ have a much steeper learning curve than many realize, just because the compilers let you get away with doing things that are fundamentally invalid (Undefined Behavior). Rust isn't actually much stricter, it just catches these problems at compile time.

Anyone capable of writing actually correct, standard-conforming C and C++ is mostly able to first-try the equivalent Rust code in almost all cases, because they are already thinking the same way that Rust requires you to think.

However, a significant portion of people who write both C and C++ don't realize that their code is full of UB - or worse, they don't care.

From a language perspective, the only new restriction in Rust compared to C++ is that mutable borrows (references) cannot overlap. Good C++ programmers are already avoiding this at all cost, because it's a mess to keep track of. When you actually do need it, Rust gives you the tools to build a safe abstraction.

EDIT: And to add, Rust is actually less restrictive in a few areas compared to C++. For example, Rust allows bitcasting between unrelated but compatible types (without going through char pointers).

text:
a well designed Rust project can leverage the type system to represent "weird states" in your program. what would otherwise be unstated rules or assumptions can be laid out cleanly as type invariants. a common example is `div(a, b) -> Option` where None is returned when b is zero. you can get really fancy with this, the blog post talks about a token struct that represents holding the GIL. doing this kind of thing can make certain logic errors more difficult to write and makes code self-documenting in some sense. going against the type system is flagged during compilation, which broadly contributes to rust code feeling like it "just works" when it compiles.

author: Xirdus
text:
Mathematically, types are sets of possible values.

Any type (like in TypeScript; Rust doesn't have one) is a set of every possible value; a supertype of all types. Every expression regardless of type can be assigned to a variable of type any.

The opposite is the never type, which is an empty set; no value is of type never. Per set theory, an empty set is a subset of every set, which makes the never type a subtype of all types. An expression of type never can be assigned to every variable regardless of type.

If never type has no values, then how can an expression have never type? Easy: it must never evaluate. Infinite loops, unconditional panics/exceptions, process exit/abort, etc. Also, generics - you can have Vec<!> that's always empty, Result<T,!> that can never be an error, etc.

author: kibwen
text: Basic use cases like that have always been possible in Rust, either via defining your own enum with zero variants (`enum Foo {}`), or by using a function return type of `!` which was hardcoded to work for certain things, e.g. infinite loops. What this release does is generalizes it so that `!` can participate in types in general, and the coolest part is that pattern matching is aware of this, so for example if you have a `Result<u8, !>` where the error variant is impossible, a `match` over this would allow you to omit the impossible error arm, and furthermore because this enum now effectively only has a single variant, it would allow you to use the pleasant irrefutable destructuring assignment syntax `let Ok(foo) = blah();`.

They are completely different release processes, for different things. C and C++ are language specifications and Rust is a tool chain. Even comparing against another compiler tool chain like gcc it wouldn't be a 1 to 1 comparison. Rust having 100 minor releases is only a factor of the passage of time.

Last time I checked between a quarter and a third had a patch release, and those are closer to a signal of "a minor release had a problem". When analysing those my conclusion and the time was "for the most part they were needed because some niche feature or platform had a regression that wasn't caught by the suite and a handful of regressions causes by enabling a new feature or updating llvm".

Even Rust Editions are not a good point of comparison because they are also time based and only leveraged by things that would otherwise be breaking changes.

What you could use for direct comparison is accepted Rust RFCs against accepted C++ proposals papers or the equivalent for other languages. Or merged Pull/Merge Request counts for the different tool chains. But that's not perfect either (Rust only supports one language, while GCC several, but it has a package manager, which GCC doesn't).
